questions.question: What is the exception class hierarchy in Java?
questions.title: Java Exception Class Hierarchy Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Throwable** is the root of all exceptions and errors in Java. It has two direct subclasses: **Error** (for serious JVM-level problems like OutOfMemoryError) and **Exception** (for recoverable conditions). **RuntimeException** extends Exception and is the parent of all unchecked exceptions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the fundamental structure of Java's exception system
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Exception is the root — freshers forget Throwable sits above everything
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Error vs Exception distinction and give a real example of each

sections.title: The Exception Hierarchy
sections.content:
In Java, every exception and error is ultimately an instance of **Throwable**. The hierarchy looks like this:

- **Throwable** (root)
  - **Error** — JVM-level problems your code normally cannot recover from (e.g., `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`)
  - **Exception** — Recoverable conditions your program can handle
    - **RuntimeException** — Unchecked exceptions (e.g., `NullPointerException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`)
    - Checked exceptions (e.g., `IOException`, `SQLException`)

The key insight: **Error** and **Exception** are siblings, both children of `Throwable`.

sections.title: Error vs Exception vs RuntimeException
sections.content:
| Aspect | Error | Checked Exception | RuntimeException |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parent | Throwable | Exception | Exception |
| Compiler check | No | Yes | No |
| Typical cause | JVM/hardware | External resources | Programming bugs |
| Example | OutOfMemoryError | IOException | NullPointerException |
| Should you catch? | Rarely | Yes | Fix the bug instead |

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: So the exception hierarchy in Java starts with **Throwable** at the very top — that's the parent of everything. Throwable has two direct children: **Error** and **Exception**. Errors are serious JVM-level problems like OutOfMemoryError — you don't usually try to catch these. Exceptions are things your program can recover from. Under Exception, we have **RuntimeException**, which is the parent of all unchecked exceptions like NullPointerException. Everything else under Exception that is not a RuntimeException is a checked exception, like IOException. So if an interviewer asks 'what is the parent of all exceptions', the technically correct answer is Throwable, not Exception.

questions.question: What is the difference between Error and Exception in Java?
questions.title: Error vs Exception in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Error** represents serious JVM-level problems (like `OutOfMemoryError`) that you normally cannot recover from, while **Exception** represents conditions an application can catch and handle. Both extend **Throwable**, but catching Errors is almost always wrong.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows which problems are program-level vs JVM-level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying you should catch Error just like Exception — that's dangerous and wrong
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention StackOverflowError as an example caused by your own code (infinite recursion)

sections.title: Error vs Exception
sections.content:
**Error** classes represent abnormal conditions in the JVM itself — things your application logic generally cannot fix:
- `OutOfMemoryError` — JVM ran out of heap space
- `StackOverflowError` — infinite recursion consumed the call stack
- `VirtualMachineError` — the JVM is broken

**Exception** classes represent conditions that a well-written application should anticipate and handle:
- `IOException` — file not found, network issue
- `NullPointerException` — programmer dereferenced null
- `SQLException` — database query failed

The key rule: **handle Exceptions, but almost never catch Errors**.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Both Error and Exception extend Throwable
- Errors signal JVM/environment problems — not program logic errors
- StackOverflowError is caused by your code (infinite recursion) but it's still an Error
- Catching Error is almost always wrong — you cannot recover from OutOfMemoryError in a catch block
- Exception is the base class for everything a normal program should handle

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: So both Error and Exception extend Throwable, but they represent very different kinds of problems. An Exception is something your program can catch and handle — like a file not being found, or a database connection failing. An Error is something much more serious, usually a JVM-level problem like running out of memory or a stack overflow. You can technically catch an Error in Java since Throwable is catchable, but you almost never should — because if the JVM is out of memory, there's nothing useful you can do inside a catch block. The general rule is: handle Exceptions, let Errors propagate or kill the process.

followup_questions: Can you give an example where catching an Error might make sense?
What is OutOfMemoryError and how do you diagnose it?

groups.heading: Error
groups.text: Error signals a JVM-level disaster your application code can't fix. OutOfMemoryError means the heap is gone. StackOverflowError means your call stack is exhausted — usually from infinite recursion. The JVM itself is in trouble, not just your logic.

groups.heading: Exception
groups.text: Exception covers conditions a well-written application should anticipate and handle. A missing file throws IOException. A bad database query throws SQLException. A null reference throws NullPointerException. These are things your code can catch and recover from.

items: Catch Exception (or its subclasses) whenever an external resource can fail — file I/O, DB, network.
Let Errors propagate unless you're a framework-level thread pool that needs to log before dying.
StackOverflowError is caused by your code but it's still an Error — fix the recursion, don't catch it.

beats.text: production trap: Catching Throwable in a REST service to 'catch everything' will silently swallow OutOfMemoryError and let the app keep running in an undefined state — serving corrupted responses until a restart.

speakable_v2.cap: Handle Exceptions because you can recover; let Errors propagate because you usually can't.

questions.question: What is RuntimeException and why is it special in the hierarchy?
questions.title: RuntimeException in Java Hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: **RuntimeException** is the parent of all **unchecked exceptions**. Its special status means the compiler does not force you to declare or catch its subclasses — unlike checked exceptions. RuntimeException subclasses typically signal programming bugs rather than external failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands why the checked/unchecked split exists
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking RuntimeException means 'exception that happens at runtime' — all exceptions happen at runtime
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that RuntimeException subclasses typically indicate programmer errors, not external failures

sections.title: Why RuntimeException is Special
sections.content:
In Java's hierarchy, the **checked vs unchecked** split is defined by one rule:

- If a class is **RuntimeException** or its subclass → **unchecked** (compiler does not force handling)
- If a class is **Exception** but NOT RuntimeException → **checked** (compiler forces handling or declaration)

**RuntimeException** was designed for programming errors — things that should not happen if the code is written correctly:
- `NullPointerException` — you accessed null
- `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` — you went past array bounds
- `IllegalArgumentException` — you passed a bad value

The philosophy: these are **bugs**. You should **fix** them, not catch them.

sections.title: RuntimeException Examples
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: So RuntimeException is a subclass of Exception, and its special role is that it's the parent of all unchecked exceptions. The name is a bit misleading because all exceptions happen at runtime — what RuntimeException really means is 'a bug in your logic'. Things like NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — those are programming mistakes. The idea is you shouldn't be catching these; you should be fixing them. The compiler agrees: it doesn't force you to handle RuntimeExceptions. If an interviewer asks 'why is it called RuntimeException', the real answer is that these are exceptions you typically only discover at runtime when the bad input or bad state actually occurs.

speakable_v2.hook: The name RuntimeException is misleading — all exceptions happen at runtime. What it really means is 'this is a bug, fix it, don't catch it'.

beats.text: RuntimeException is a direct subclass of Exception and the parent of every unchecked exception. Being a RuntimeException subclass tells the compiler: don't force callers to handle this. It's Java's way of categorizing bugs — things that shouldn't happen in correct code.

If the compiler forced you to catch every NullPointerException or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, your code would be buried in try-catch blocks. These are bugs — the right response is to fix the code, not to catch the symptom everywhere.

items: Unchecked — compiler doesn't require try-catch or throws declaration
Signals programming errors — null access, bad array index, wrong cast, illegal argument
Custom unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException — e.g., UserNotFoundException in a Spring service

beats.text: non-obvious: In a Java 17 REST service, UserNotFoundException extends RuntimeException so it can propagate freely through service and controller layers without polluting every method signature with throws. Spring's @ControllerAdvice catches it at the top and returns a 404.

items: Thinking RuntimeException means it only happens at runtime — all exceptions do; the name means unchecked.
Catching RuntimeException broadly with catch(RuntimeException e) — masks bugs instead of fixing them.
Making every custom exception extend RuntimeException blindly — some failures genuinely warrant checked exceptions.

speakable_v2.cap: RuntimeException defines the unchecked branch — it's for bugs you should fix, not failures you should catch.

questions.question: What methods does the Throwable class provide?
questions.title: Throwable Class Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Throwable** provides the core infrastructure for exceptions: **getMessage()** for the error description, **getCause()** for exception chaining, **printStackTrace()** to print the call stack, and **getStackTrace()** to access stack frames programmatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding — does the candidate know what Throwable actually provides
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing getCause() exists or what exception chaining means
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention exception chaining via getCause() and why it matters for debugging in production

sections.title: Key Throwable Methods
sections.content:
**Throwable** provides these key capabilities:

- **getMessage()** — human-readable description of the error
- **getCause()** — the original exception that triggered this one (exception chaining)
- **printStackTrace()** — prints the full call stack to stderr
- **getStackTrace()** — returns stack trace as an array for programmatic logging
- **toString()** — class name + message

Exception chaining via `getCause()` is especially important. When you catch an `IOException` and wrap it in a `ServiceException`, you pass the original as the cause so the full story is preserved.

sections.title: Exception Chaining with getCause()
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Throwable gives you the core plumbing for all exceptions: getMessage() for the error description, printStackTrace() so you can see the full call stack, and getCause() which enables exception chaining. Exception chaining is really useful — say you catch a low-level SQLException and want to throw a higher-level ServiceException. You pass the original SQLException as the cause. Now anyone who catches your ServiceException can still see the underlying database error by calling getCause(). That's important for debugging in production because you don't lose the original error information.

followup_questions: What is exception chaining and why is it useful?
What is the difference between getMessage() and toString() on an exception?
When would you use getStackTrace() instead of printStackTrace()?

beats.text: Throwable is the root of Java's exception system and provides all the core plumbing: ways to get the error message, inspect the call stack, and trace back to the original cause. Every exception you'll ever throw or catch inherits these methods automatically.

Without Throwable's methods, exceptions would just be labels with no diagnostic information. getMessage, getCause, and getStackTrace are what make exceptions useful for debugging rather than just crashing.

items: getMessage() — the human-readable description you pass to the constructor
getCause() — the original exception that triggered this one; enables exception chaining
printStackTrace() — prints the full call stack to stderr; useful in development
getStackTrace() — returns stack frames as an array; useful for structured logging in production
toString() — class name plus message; what you see in logs without the full trace

beats.text: sharp edge: In a Java 17 REST service, when you catch a SQLException and wrap it in a ServiceException, always pass the original as the cause. In production, calling getCause() on the ServiceException reveals the exact SQL error — without it, you only see the high-level message and lose the root cause entirely.

items: Using printStackTrace() in production — it prints to stderr, not your log framework; use a logger instead.
Wrapping without passing the cause — getCause() returns null and the original stack trace is gone.
Confusing getMessage() with toString() — toString() includes the class name, getMessage() is just the text.

speakable_v2.cap: Know all five methods, but getCause() is the one that proves you understand exception chaining.

questions.question: Can you catch multiple exceptions in a single catch block in Java?
questions.title: Multi-Catch Exception Handling in Java 7
questions.direct_answer: Yes. Since **Java 7**, you can catch multiple exception types in a single `catch` block using the **pipe operator** (`|`). This is called **multi-catch** and reduces duplicated handling code. The caught variable is implicitly **final** and the two types cannot be in a parent-child relationship.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing separate catch blocks for exceptions that share identical handling logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the variable is implicitly final in multi-catch, preventing reassignment

sections.title: Multi-Catch Syntax
Key Points
sections.content:
- Multi-catch uses | between exception types (not &&, not comma)
- The caught variable is implicitly final — you cannot reassign it in the block
- The two types cannot be in a parent-child relationship (compile error)
- Reduces code duplication when different exceptions have identical handling
- Available since Java 7

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Yes, since Java 7 you can catch multiple exceptions in a single catch block using the pipe operator. So instead of writing two catch blocks that do exactly the same thing, you write catch IOException or SQLException and handle both in one place. One thing worth mentioning: the exception variable in a multi-catch is implicitly final, so you can't reassign it inside the block. Also, you can't catch two exceptions where one is a parent of the other — so catch Exception or IOException won't compile because IOException is already an Exception. This feature is mainly useful for reducing duplicated error-handling code.

followup_questions: Why is the exception variable final in a multi-catch block?
What happens if you try to catch Exception | IOException in a multi-catch?
How is multi-catch different from catching the common parent exception?

Before Java 7, if IOException and SQLException needed identical handling, you wrote two identical catch blocks. That's copy-paste code waiting to become inconsistent. Multi-catch removes that duplication cleanly.

beats.text: candidates miss: You can't write catch(Exception | IOException e) because IOException is already a subclass of Exception — the compiler rejects it as redundant. The pipe only works for exception types that are genuinely independent in the hierarchy.

Using multi-catch when exceptions need different handling — stick to separate blocks in that case.

questions.question: Does the finally block run even when an exception is not caught?
questions.title: Finally Block Execution Without Catch
questions.direct_answer: Yes. The **finally block always runs** — even when the exception is not caught and propagates up the call stack. The finally block executes before the exception continues propagating. The only exceptions: `System.exit()` or a JVM crash.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of finally block semantics — a common output-prediction question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking finally only runs when an exception is caught
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention System.exit() as the case where finally does NOT run, and the gotcha if finally itself throws

sections.title: Output Prediction
Finally Always Runs
sections.content:
The **finally block runs before the exception propagates**, regardless of whether there is a catch block. This is by design — finally is for cleanup code (closing resources, releasing locks) that must execute no matter what.

Exceptions to the 'always runs' rule:
1. `System.exit()` is called inside try/catch — the JVM terminates immediately
2. The JVM itself crashes (kill -9 on the process)

Gotcha: **if finally itself throws an exception, it replaces the original exception** — the original is silently swallowed.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Yes, the finally block always runs — even when the exception isn't caught. The sequence is: try block executes, exception is thrown, Java checks for a matching catch, doesn't find one, but before propagating up to the caller it runs the finally block. After finally completes, the exception continues propagating. The only time finally doesn't run is if you call System.exit() or the JVM crashes. There's also a subtle gotcha: if the finally block itself throws an exception, that new exception replaces the original one, and you lose the original exception information entirely.

followup_questions: What happens if finally throws an exception?

speakable_v2.hook: Finally doesn't care whether an exception was caught. It runs anyway — that's the whole point of guaranteed cleanup.

beats.text: The finally block is Java's guarantee of cleanup. It runs after the try (and catch, if present) regardless of what happened — exception thrown, exception caught, or normal exit. It's designed for code that must execute no matter the outcome.

Without finally, cleanup code like closing connections or releasing locks would only run on the happy path. If an exception skipped past it, you'd have resource leaks. Finally was designed to close that gap.

items: Runs after try completes — whether normally or by exception
Runs even when no catch block matches the exception
Does NOT run if System.exit() is called or the JVM crashes
If finally itself throws, the original exception is silently replaced

beats.text: sharp edge: If your finally block throws a new exception, Java discards the original exception completely. In a Java 17 service, if close() on a resource throws inside finally, you lose the original failure reason — one reason try-with-resources is preferred over manual finally blocks.

items: Putting a return statement in finally — it overrides the try block's return value silently.
Assuming finally doesn't run without a catch — it runs even with zero catch blocks.
Letting finally throw — it silently swallows the original exception you actually need to diagnose.

speakable_v2.cap: Finally always runs for cleanup — except System.exit() — and if it throws, the original exception is gone.
